ai.definition: 2D materials refer to substances that are two-dimensional, typically consisting of a single layer or a few layers of atoms. These include graphene, which is composed of carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, and borophene, an allotrope of boron with similar properties but distinct atomic structure.
ai.howItWorks: These materials exhibit unique electronic, mechanical, and optical properties due to their atom-thin layers, making them highly sought after for applications such as electronics, energy storage, and composite materials. The exceptional properties arise from the quantum confinement effects at the nanoscale, leading to novel physical phenomena.
ai.problemSolved: Traditional materials often face limitations in performance or cost, especially when it comes to miniaturization in electronic devices. 2D materials offer a solution by providing superior electrical conductivity, thermal stability, and mechanical strength, enabling the development of more efficient and smaller-scale technologies.
ai.manufacturing: The production of 2D materials involves various techniques such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD), epitaxial growth on substrates, and exfoliation from bulk crystals. These processes are complex and require precise control over temperature, pressure, and gas flow to achieve high-quality layers.
ai.buildProcess: The build process for devices using 2D materials typically involves depositing the material onto a substrate, patterning it into functional structures (e.g., transistors), and integrating it with other components. This often requires advanced fabrication techniques like lithography, etching, and deposition methods.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the complexity of production processes, the need for high-purity materials, and the requirement for specialized equipment. Additionally, scaling up manufacturing to meet demand remains a significant challenge.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive as research and development continue to advance the understanding and practical applications of these materials. However, widespread adoption faces hurdles related to cost and scalability.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks for 2D materials are still evolving. Safety concerns regarding potential environmental impacts and human exposure need to be addressed through stringent testing and standards.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the difficulty in achieving consistent quality across large-scale production, as well as integration challenges with existing technologies. Economic risks stem from high initial costs and uncertain market demand.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable depending on specific applications and market conditions. High-performance electronics and energy storage devices show potential for significant economic benefits but require substantial investment in R&D and manufacturing infrastructure.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving production techniques, reducing costs, and expanding the range of practical applications. Collaboration between academia and industry is crucial to drive innovation.

glossary.def: Materials with a thickness on the order of nanometers, typically consisting of a single layer or few layers of atoms.
A two-dimensional material made from carbon atoms arranged in a hexagonal lattice, known for its exceptional electrical and thermal conductivity.
An allotrope of boron with a unique atomic structure that offers promising properties for various applications.
A process used to deposit thin films or layers by the reaction of gaseous precursors on a substrate.
The growth of one crystalline material onto another, resulting in a crystal structure that is aligned with the underlying substrate.

subsystems.name: Feedstock
subsystems.role: supplies the atoms that become the atom-thin layer.

subsystems.name: Growth surface
subsystems.role: the template whose crystal structure decides how the layer forms.

subsystems.name: Reactor
subsystems.role: provides the heat, vacuum and gas flow needed for growth.

subsystems.name: Transfer and handling
subsystems.role: moves a fragile one-atom-thick sheet onto a useful substrate.

subsystems.name: Characterisation
subsystems.role: checks thickness, crystal quality and defects.

subsystems.name: Device integration
subsystems.role: turns the sheet into working components.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the growth surface
buildSteps.detail: Copper foil is cleaned, electropolished and annealed so its grains are large and flat; for borophene, a silver (111) crystal is polished and cleaned in ultrahigh vacuum.

buildSteps.title: Grow the layer
buildSteps.detail: In chemical vapour deposition, methane and hydrogen flow over hot copper (about 1000 °C) and carbon atoms assemble into a hexagonal sheet. Borophene instead forms by evaporating boron onto silver (111) in ultrahigh vacuum, a method first reported in 2015.

buildSteps.title: Cool and stabilise
buildSteps.detail: The layer is cooled under controlled gas flow; cooling rate and pressure determine wrinkles and the number of layers. Borophene must stay in vacuum, as it oxidises in air.

buildSteps.title: Transfer the sheet
buildSteps.detail: A polymer film is spin-coated on top, the metal beneath is etched away, the floating film is fished onto the target substrate, and the polymer is dissolved.

buildSteps.title: Measure and inspect
buildSteps.detail: Raman spectroscopy, electron microscopy and scanning probe techniques confirm the layer count and reveal grain boundaries and holes.

buildSteps.title: Pattern and contact
buildSteps.detail: Lithography defines device shapes, metal is deposited for electrical contacts, and unwanted material is etched away.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate and stack
buildSteps.detail: Hexagonal boron nitride or another insulator is placed on top, and several 2D layers can be stacked at controlled twist angles to build new electronic and optical behaviour.

buildSteps.title: Scale up
buildSteps.detail: Roll-to-roll chemical vapour deposition has demonstrated metre-scale graphene on metal foil; wafer-scale growth on silicon carbide is used for some electronic grades.

prerequisites.tech: Large-area chemical vapour deposition on metal foils
prerequisites.why: roll-to-roll production has shown metre-scale graphene, the basis for any bulk application.
borophene and similar materials form only on clean single-crystal surfaces in extreme vacuum, so far only at laboratory scale.
moving the sheet from its growth surface usually introduces tears, wrinkles and polymer residue that degrade performance.
industry needs to certify billions of identical devices, which requires fast, reliable inspection across a whole wafer.
pristine graphene conducts at all voltages, so it cannot simply be switched off like a semiconductor.
borophene and many related materials oxidise within minutes, which rules out ordinary device fabrication unless they are protected.

pathway.milestone: graphene powders and inks used in composites, batteries, thermal films and some sensors
pathway.unlocks: real markets that fund the more demanding electronics work.

pathway.milestone: wafer-scale graphene for radio-frequency circuits, photonics and gas sensing
pathway.unlocks: devices that exploit graphene's speed and sensitivity without needing a bandgap.

pathway.milestone: reliable stacks of graphene, boron nitride and other 2D layers
pathway.unlocks: tunnelling transistors, memory and optoelectronic devices with properties silicon cannot match.

pathway.milestone: air-stable 2D metals such as borophene integrated into working circuits
pathway.unlocks: atom-thin conductors and catalysts, and a possible route beyond silicon transistors.
